title: Jesus Prays for Himself, His Disciples, and All Believers
summary: At the end of the farewell discourse Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays. He asks the Father to glorify the Son now that the hour has come, as he has glorified the Father by finishing the work he was given. He prays for his disciples, that the Father would keep them in his name, protect them from the evil one, and sanctify them by the truth as he sends them into the world. Finally he prays for all who will believe through their message, that they may be one as the Father and the Son are one, and that they may be with him to see his glory.
story:
Chapters 13 to 16 were Jesus speaking to his disciples; chapter 17 is Jesus speaking to his Father, with the disciples listening. It is the longest prayer of Jesus recorded in the Gospels and the climax of the farewell discourse. Immediately after it Jesus crosses the Kidron Valley to the garden where he will be arrested (18:1). The prayer therefore stands at the threshold of the passion, and in it Jesus gives his own account of what he has done and what he is about to do. The hour that had not yet come at Cana (2:4) and in Jerusalem (7:30, 8:20), and that he announced in 12:23, has now arrived: “Father, the hour has come” (verse 1).

Nearly every theme of the Gospel is gathered here and offered back to God: the glory the Word had with the Father before creation (1:1, 1:14), eternal life (3:16), the work the Father gave the Son to finish (4:34, 5:36), the name of God made known, the people given to the Son (6:37-39), the world that hates and yet is loved, the sending of the Son and now of the disciples, the unity of the scattered children of God (11:52), and the love of the Father for the Son. Where the other Gospels show Jesus in anguish in Gethsemane, John gives the reader this prayer of calm confidence; the two do not cancel each other, since John also records that Jesus' soul was troubled at the approach of the hour (12:27).
historical:
The prayer is spoken in Jerusalem on the night before Jesus' crucifixion under Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judea from about AD 26 to 36, at the time of Passover. Since the sixteenth century it has usually been called the High Priestly Prayer, a title traced to the Lutheran theologian David Chytraeus (1531 to 1600), though the idea of Jesus acting as priest in this chapter is much older: Cyril of Alexandria's Commentary on John, in the early fifth century, already speaks of Christ here as mediator, high priest, and advocate for his people.

The title reflects a real pattern. On the Day of Atonement Israel's high priest made atonement first for himself and his household and then for the whole assembly of Israel (Leviticus 16:6, 16:11, 16:17). The Mishnah's description of the day, compiled around AD 200 but preserving memories of temple practice, gives the order of his confessions: for himself and his house (m. Yoma 3:8), then for himself, his house, and the priests, the sons of Aaron (m. Yoma 4:2), and then for all Israel (m. Yoma 6:2). In each confession the high priest spoke the divine name, and the Mishnah says that when the priests and people in the court heard the name come from his mouth, they bowed down (m. Yoma 6:2). Jesus' prayer moves in a similar widening circle, first concerning himself, then for the disciples, then for all who will believe, and it is saturated with the name of God, which Jesus says he has made known and in which he asks that his people be kept (verses 6, 11, 12, 26). He also says that he sanctifies himself for them (verse 19), the language used for consecrating priests (Exodus 28:41, 29:1) and sacrifices (Deuteronomy 15:19). No text says that John had the Day of Atonement in mind, and the link is a pattern rather than an explicit claim, but it explains why the title has endured.

Farewell prayers also belonged to the form of the farewell speech. Moses ends his last words with a blessing on the tribes (Deuteronomy 33), and in Jubilees, a retelling of Genesis from the second century BC, Abraham prays for Jacob and his descendants before his death (Jubilees 22:10-24). Paul, taking leave of the Ephesian elders, commits them to God and kneels to pray with them (Acts 20:32-36). John's readers late in the first century, spread across the Roman world and including Jews and Gentiles, stood among “those who will believe in Me through their message” (verse 20), and the prayer for their unity addressed a live concern, as Paul's letters show (1 Corinthians 1:10-13, Ephesians 2:11-22).
cultural:
Jesus prays looking up to heaven (verse 1), as he did at Lazarus's tomb (11:41). Lifting the eyes was a common posture of prayer (Psalm 121:1, 123:1), and its opposite, the tax collector who would not lift his eyes (Luke 18:13), shows what it meant. Jews usually prayed standing, though John does not say whether Jesus stood or where exactly he was. He addresses God simply as Father, as he does throughout John, and also as Holy Father (verse 11) and Righteous Father (verse 25). Jewish prayer commonly named God by his character at the start of a petition, and both titles suit what follows: the holy Father is asked to keep his people and set them apart, the righteous Father is appealed to over against a world that has not known him.

In the Bible a name stands for the person's character, reputation, and presence. God chose a place for his name to dwell (Deuteronomy 12:11, 1 Kings 8:29), and the prophets promised a day when his people would know his name (Isaiah 52:6). When Jesus says he has revealed the Father's name (verse 6) and asks that the disciples be kept in the name the Father gave him (verses 11 and 12), he means that he has made God himself known and that God's own character and power will guard them. That the Father has given the name to the Son is a striking claim in a Jewish setting, where the divine name was treated with the greatest reverence; Paul says something similar when he writes that God gave Jesus the name above every name (Philippians 2:9).

To sanctify (hagiazō) is to set apart as holy for God's use. In Israel priests, sacrifices, the firstborn, the sabbath, and the temple vessels were sanctified. The prophets were also set apart for their mission (Jeremiah 1:5), and Jesus has already described himself as the one “whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world” (10:36). Here the disciples are sanctified by the truth, which is the Father's word (verse 17), for the purpose of being sent (verse 18). Holiness in this chapter is not withdrawal from the world but consecration for mission within it. Knowing God (verse 3) also had a covenantal sense in Israel's Scriptures, where to know the LORD means to acknowledge and belong to him (Jeremiah 31:34, Hosea 6:6), and the Wisdom of Solomon says that to know God is complete righteousness and the root of immortality (Wisdom 15:3).
literary:
The prayer has three movements, marked by whom Jesus prays for: concerning himself and his glory (verses 1 to 5), for the disciples he is leaving in the world (6 to 19), and for all who will believe through their word (20 to 26). Some commentators divide the middle section at verse 9, where Jesus says I ask on their behalf, and others at verse 11, where the petitions begin, but the threefold widening is plain. The prayer uses the same circling style as the discourse, in which each petition returns to earlier themes and carries them further.

A few words bind the whole. World (kosmos) occurs eighteen times and carries its full Johannine range: the created order that existed after the Son's glory (verse 5), humanity out of which the disciples were given (verse 6), the hostile system that hates them (verse 14), and the mission field into which they are sent and which may yet believe (verses 18, 21, 23). Give (didōmi) occurs seventeen times: the Father gives the Son authority, people, work, words, a name, and glory, and the Son gives the disciples eternal life, the Father's word, and glory. Glory and glorify, name, know, send, keep, and one recur throughout. Verse 3 is unusual in that Jesus names himself in the third person as Jesus Christ; many commentators think it reads like the evangelist's own summary of the Gospel's message woven into the prayer, while others see it as a natural confessional formula on Jesus' lips.

Many readers have noticed how closely the prayer's concerns track the Lord's Prayer in Matthew and Luke. Jesus addresses God as Father, asks that the Father be glorified as the other prayer asks that his name be hallowed, speaks of completing the work the Father gave, which corresponds to the Father's will being done, and asks that the disciples be kept from the evil one (verse 15), the same phrase as the last petition in Matthew 6:13. Raymond Brown drew attention to these parallels in his commentary. The prayer ends not with a request but with a promise, that Jesus will continue to make the Father's name known so that the Father's love for the Son may be in them, and he in them (verse 26), a closing that turns the prayer outward to the Gospel's readers.

outline.t: Jesus prays for his own glorification
Jesus prays for all who will believe

doctrines.note: Jesus speaks of “the glory I had with You before the world existed” (verse 5) and of the Father's love for him “before the foundation of the world” (verse 24). The Son's relationship with the Father is eternal, and it is a relationship of mutual indwelling and shared possession: “All I have is Yours, and all You have is Mine” (verse 10). The fourth-century church drew on the chapter in confessing the Son as eternally one with the Father, even while debating verse 3.

The prayer opens by asking the Father to glorify the Son so that the Son may glorify the Father (verse 1). In John the hour of glory is the hour of the cross, resurrection, and return to the Father, where God's love and faithfulness are shown in full. Jesus has glorified the Father by finishing his work (verse 4), he gives his glory to his people (verse 22), and he wills that they be with him to see it (verse 24).

The chapter presents Christ in his priestly office. He intercedes for his people, consecrates himself for them (verse 19), and asks that they be kept, sanctified, united, and brought to his glory. The New Testament presents the risen Christ as continuing this intercession at the Father's right hand (Romans 8:34, Hebrews 7:25, 1 John 2:1), and Hebrews develops at length the priesthood this prayer displays.

“Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth” (verse 17). The Father sets his people apart through his word, for the purpose of sending them into the world (verse 18), and their sanctification rests on Christ's consecrating himself for them (verse 19). Holiness here is not withdrawal but belonging to God in the middle of a world that hates them.

Jesus prays for all who will believe through the apostles' message, that they may be one as the Father and the Son are one, “so that the world may believe that You sent Me” (verse 21). The unity of believers is modeled on and grounded in the unity of the Father and the Son, it has a witnessing purpose, and it stands as both a gift to receive and a judgment on the church's divisions.

words.note: Doxazō, to glorify, honor, make glorious. It occurs about 61 times in the New Testament and 23 in John, five of them in this chapter. In ordinary Greek it meant to hold an opinion or to praise, but through the Greek Old Testament's use of doxa for the radiant presence of God it came to mean to reveal someone's true weight and splendor. In John the Son is glorified in the hour of his death and exaltation (12:23, 13:31-32), the Father is glorified in the Son's obedience, and the disciples glorify both by bearing fruit (15:8).

Ginōskō, to know. It occurs about 222 times in the New Testament and some 57 times in John, seven in this chapter. In verse 3 eternal life is defined as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. Biblical knowing is relational and covenantal rather than merely intellectual: the Hebrew yada can describe the intimacy of marriage and God's choosing of Israel (Amos 3:2). John never uses the noun gnōsis, knowledge, perhaps because it was already prized by teachers who made salvation a matter of secret insight; he prefers the verb, which names a living relationship.

Apostellō, to send with a commission. It occurs about 132 times in the New Testament and about 28 in John, seven in this chapter, where it always describes the Father sending the Son, except once: “As You sent Me into the world, I have also sent them into the world” (verse 18). John also uses pempō for sending, and the two are largely interchangeable in his usage. The related noun apostolos, one who is sent, gives us the word apostle. The sending of the disciples is patterned on and derived from the sending of the Son, a thought the risen Jesus repeats in 20:21.

Onoma, name. It occurs over 200 times in the New Testament, four times in this chapter. In Hebrew thought a name expresses character and presence, and the divine name marked God's self-revelation to Moses (Exodus 3:13-15, 34:5-7). Jesus says he has revealed the Father's name (verses 6 and 26) and speaks of the name the Father gave him (verses 11 and 12). The phrase suggests that the Son bears God's own name, a claim that fits the I am sayings of the Gospel (8:58) and Paul's confession in Philippians 2:9-11.

Tēreō, to keep, guard, protect, observe. It occurs about 70 times in the New Testament and 18 in John. It can mean to keep a command (verse 6, where the disciples have kept the Father's word) or to guard a person (verses 11, 12, 15). The two senses meet in this chapter: those who keep the Father's word are kept by the Father's name. In verse 12 Jesus uses it alongside phulassō, to guard, of his protection of the disciples while he was with them. The verb does not promise that they will be taken out of the world, only that they will be guarded in it.

Hagiazō, to sanctify, make holy, consecrate. It occurs 28 times in the New Testament and four in John (10:36; 17:17, 19 twice). In the Greek Old Testament it is used for consecrating priests, altars, sacrifices, and firstborn animals to God. Jesus asks the Father to sanctify the disciples in the truth (verse 17) and says, “For them I sanctify Myself” (verse 19). Many interpreters, from John Chrysostom onward, have heard in this the language of sacrifice: Jesus consecrates himself to death so that his people may be set apart for God.

Teleioō, to complete, finish, bring to its goal, perfect. It occurs 23 times in the New Testament, nine in Hebrews and five in John. Jesus speaks of completing the work the Father gave him (4:34, 5:36, 17:4), and at the cross John uses the word for the Scripture being brought to its fulfillment when Jesus says “I am thirsty” (19:28). In verse 23 it describes believers being brought to complete unity, literally perfected into one. The same goal-directed word joins Jesus' finished work and his people's unity.

Apōleia, destruction, ruin, perdition. It occurs 18 times in the New Testament. The phrase son of destruction (verse 12) is a Hebrew idiom in which son of means belonging to or destined for, as in sons of disobedience (Ephesians 2:2); it describes Judas as one who belongs to destruction. Paul uses the same phrase of the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3). There is a wordplay in the verse: none of them was lost (apōleto) except the son of apōleia.

christ:
This chapter lets the reader overhear the Son speaking with the Father on the eve of the cross, and more of who Christ is appears here than almost anywhere in the Gospels. He shared glory with the Father before the world existed (verse 5) and was loved by him before the foundation of the world (verse 24), so the prayer confirms the prologue's confession that the Word was with God and was God (1:1). He has authority over all flesh to give eternal life (verse 2), a prerogative of God alone. He possesses all that the Father has (verse 10) and bears the Father's name (verses 11 and 12).

He is also the obedient Son who has finished the work he was given (verse 4), and the great high priest who consecrates himself as the offering (verse 19) and intercedes for his people. The letter to the Hebrews develops the same portrait: a high priest who offered himself once for all and always lives to make intercession (Hebrews 7:25, 9:11-14). Israel's high priest bore the names of the tribes on his breastpiece before the LORD (Exodus 28:29), and here Jesus bears his people before the Father by name and by gift: those you have given me.

The prayer also shows the goal of his work. The shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep promised to gather other sheep into one flock (10:16), and John has said that he would die to gather into one the scattered children of God (11:52). Here that gathering becomes prayer: that all who believe may be one, in the Father and the Son, and that the world may believe. The end of the story is not only forgiveness but presence: that his people may be with him where he is and see his glory (verse 24), which the last chapters of the Bible picture as God dwelling with his people and their seeing his face (Revelation 21:3, 22:4). The prayer is still being answered, since every generation of believers stands among those who believe through the apostles' message.
interpretation:
The prayer has been read in every age of the church as a window into the life of God. Augustine's Tractates on John 104 to 111 cover it, ending with a meditation on verse 24 and the promise that believers will be with Christ where he is. The fourth-century debates over the Son's deity made verse 3 contested ground. Arian writers cited the only true God as proof that the Son was not true God. Augustine (Tractate 105) answered that the sentence should be construed as knowing the Father and Jesus Christ whom he sent together as the only true God, and others read the phrase as distinguishing the one God from idols rather than the Father from the Son. John Chrysostom (Homilies 80 to 82 on John) observed that after warning the disciples of tribulation Jesus turned to prayer, raising their spirits and teaching believers to flee to God in their own trials. Cyril of Alexandria, in the eleventh book of his Commentary on John, read verses 20 to 23 as teaching that believers are made one both through the Spirit and through sharing in the one body of Christ in the Eucharist, and he spoke of Christ in this chapter as mediator, high priest, and advocate.

Thomas Aquinas's lectures on John read the prayer as offered by Christ in his human nature to the Father. Martin Luther preached on the chapter in 1528 and published the sermons in 1530, treating it as the heart of Christ's priestly office and a comfort for troubled consciences, and the name High Priestly Prayer is traced to the Lutheran theologian David Chytraeus later in that century. Calvin's commentary (1553) read the son of destruction in verse 12 in the light of his doctrine of election, which has kept the verse at the center of debate about Judas.

Modern scholarship has disagreed sharply about the chapter. Rudolf Bultmann's commentary (1941) moved the prayer to follow the supper and Judas's departure (13:1-30), before the discourses, as part of his rearrangement of chapters 13 to 16. Ernst Käsemann's The Testament of Jesus (German 1966, English 1968), given first as lectures at Yale, argued from chapter 17 that John's Christ is a God striding over the earth whose humanity is hardly more than a backdrop, a charge Marianne Meye Thompson answered in The Humanity of Jesus in the Fourth Gospel (1988). D. A. Carson's The Farewell Discourse and Final Prayer of Jesus (1980) gave the chapter an extended evangelical exposition.

Verse 21 became the charter of the modern movement for Christian unity. The Latin Ut omnes unum sint, that all may be one, is the motto of the United Church of Canada, formed by union in 1925, and of the World Student Christian Federation. William Turton's hymn Thou, who at thy first Eucharist didst pray (1881) turns the chapter into a prayer for the church's unity. The Second Vatican Council's decree on ecumenism, Unitatis Redintegratio (1964), and John Paul II's encyclical Ut Unum Sint (1995), which takes its title from verse 21, both ground Catholic ecumenism in this prayer, and the Lausanne Covenant (1974) affirmed that the church's visible unity in truth is God's purpose. In worship, the Revised Common Lectionary reads the chapter on the seventh Sunday of Easter in all three years: verses 1 to 11 in Year A, 6 to 19 in Year B, and 20 to 26 in Year C. In the Orthodox Church the chapter belongs to the first of the Twelve Passion Gospels read on Holy Thursday evening, and 17:1-13 is read on the Sunday after the Ascension, which commemorates the fathers of the Council of Nicaea.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles here come from manuscripts. In verses 11 and 12 the best manuscripts read that the Father should keep the disciples in your name which you have given me, meaning that the Father has given his name to the Son; later manuscripts read keep in your name those whom you have given me, and so the King James Version has ‘keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me’ (verse 11) and ‘those that thou gavest me I have kept’ (verse 12). Modern versions follow the older reading, which carries a high claim about the Son. In verse 21 later manuscripts add the word one, ‘that they also may be one in us’ (KJV), where the earlier text reads that they may also be in us. In verse 24 the earliest manuscripts use a neuter singular, literally ‘what you have given me’, where later manuscripts have a masculine plural, ‘those whom’; the neuter, found also in verse 2, presents the disciples as a single gift from the Father, and most modern versions translate it as a plural for clarity.

There are also translation differences. In verse 15 the Greek tou ponērou can mean either the evil one (BSB, ESV, NIV) or evil in general (KJV's ‘from the evil’); the masculine sense matches 1 John 2:13-14 and 5:18-19. The KJV's ‘son of perdition’ (verse 12) and modern versions' ‘son of destruction’ render the same phrase. The Scripture fulfilled in verse 12 is most often taken to be Psalm 41:9, already quoted in 13:18, which is verse 10 in the Hebrew Bible and Psalm 40:10 in the Greek Old Testament's numbering; some interpreters also think of Psalm 109:8, applied to Judas in Acts 1:20.

teach.big: On the eve of the cross the Son asks the Father to glorify him and to keep, sanctify, unite, and finally gather to his glory the people the Father has given him, and his prayer is the ground of the church's life and mission in the world.

outline.t: The hour of the cross is the hour of glory, and eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent.
Jesus finished the work the Father gave him and returns to the glory he shared with the Father before creation.
The disciples belong to the Father, were given to the Son, and have received and kept the Father's word through him.
Jesus prays for his own, asking the holy Father to keep them in his name so that they may be one, as he kept them while he was with them.
Jesus wants his joy in his people, and he asks not that they be taken out of a hostile world but that they be kept from the evil one within it.
God's word sets his people apart for mission, and their holiness rests on Christ's consecrating himself for them.
Every later believer is included in this prayer, and the unity Jesus asks for is modeled on the Father and the Son and meant to show the world that God sent him and loves them.
The goal of the whole story is to be with Christ and see his glory, and he continues to make the Father's name known so that the Father's love may live in his people.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first reduces unity in verses 20 to 23 either to institutional merger or to an invisible spiritual unity that asks nothing visible of anyone. The unity Jesus prays for is grounded in the Father and the Son and in the apostolic word (verse 20), and it is meant to be seen, so that the world may believe. Teachers should let it judge every tradition's divisions, not only the other side's. The second uses verse 3 to deny the deity of Christ, or, from the other direction, passes over it too quickly. The verse distinguishes the true God from idols and joins Jesus Christ to him as the one through whom he is known; it is best read with verses 5 and 24.

The third turns in the world but not of the world (verses 14 to 18) into a slogan for either withdrawal or cultural accommodation. Jesus explicitly refuses to ask that his people be taken out of the world and sends them into it, and he defines their difference from it by the Father's word and the truth, not by style or subculture. The fourth reads verse 12 as fatalism, as though Judas were a puppet whose betrayal proves God's cruelty, or conversely ignores it; see the hard question below. The fifth makes this a prayer only for the eleven or only for clergy. Verse 20 includes every believer in every age.

Finally, beware of treating the prayer mainly as an example of how to pray. It does model prayer, but it is first a unique act of the Son on the night of his passion, and its central petitions concern what only he can ask and accomplish.
teach.pastoral: The prayer offers deep comfort to people who fear they will not hold on. Jesus asks the Father to keep his people and says that none of those given to him has been lost (verse 12); the anxious and the scrupulous need to hear that their perseverance rests in part on his prayer, not only on their grip. The mention of Judas may unsettle such people, and it should be handled gently: the text holds Judas responsible and does not invite anyone to wonder whether they are secretly doomed. Those who have been wounded by church splits, abusive leaders, or the hostility of other Christians may find verses 20 to 23 painful, since the church's divisions have hurt them personally; the prayer names what Jesus desires, and its failure in practice is a cause for grief and repentance rather than for cynicism. People who feel out of place in a hostile workplace or family may take courage from verses 14 to 18: Jesus neither pulls his people out nor leaves them unguarded.

hard.q: If Judas was lost “so that the Scripture would be fulfilled,” did he have any choice?
hard.a:
The objection is old and strong. If Scripture foretold the betrayal and Jesus calls Judas the son of destruction (verse 12), then Judas seems to have been cast in a part he could not refuse, and to condemn him for playing it looks unjust. Critics have pressed the point in different ways. Hyam Maccoby (Judas Iscariot and the Myth of Jewish Evil, 1992) argued that the figure of the evil Judas grew in the later Gospels, John most of all, and served to embody Christian hostility toward Jews, his very name echoing Judah. William Klassen (Judas: Betrayer or Friend of Jesus?, 1996) argued that the earliest sources describe Judas as handing Jesus over, possibly without malice, and that the portrait darkens over time. The Gospel of Judas, a second-century text known to Irenaeus (Against Heresies 1.31.1) and published from the Codex Tchacos in 2006, went further and made Judas the one disciple who understood Jesus and did what he asked.

Christian responses have taken several forms. Augustine and the Reformed tradition hold that God ordained the betrayal within his purpose while Judas acted willingly and bore full guilt, in the way Acts 2:23 says Jesus was handed over by God's set purpose and foreknowledge and yet by lawless hands. Calvin read verse 12 in that light. Arminian and many other interpreters hold that God foreknew what Judas would freely choose and that Scripture foretold it without causing it, so that the Scripture was fulfilled in Judas rather than forcing him. Many commentators add that Psalm 41:9, quoted in 13:18, describes a recurring pattern, the righteous sufferer betrayed by a trusted friend, which Judas fulfilled by his own choices, as Ahithophel had betrayed David (2 Samuel 15 to 17). Karl Barth, in Church Dogmatics II/2 (1942), devoted a long discussion to Judas as the representative of the rejected whom Christ himself bore, a reading that has moved some to hope for Judas and others to criticize Barth for blurring the line the Gospels draw.

The Gospel itself presents Judas as responsible. John records his theft (12:6) and the devil's influence (13:2, 13:27), yet Jesus washes his feet and gives him the morsel, gestures of love to the end. On Maccoby's and Klassen's historical reconstructions, many scholars reply that Judas's betrayal is attested in every Gospel and in Paul's reference to the night Jesus was handed over (1 Corinthians 11:23), and that the church, not the text, bears the blame for turning Judas into a symbol of the Jewish people. How God's purposes and human freedom fit together is a question on which faithful Christians have long differed, and the Bible affirms both without fully explaining them.

hard.q: Jesus prayed that his followers would be one. Doesn't the divided church show that his prayer failed?
hard.a:
The objection is as old as the second century. The pagan critic Celsus mocked the Christians for splitting into rival factions that condemned one another, and Origen quoted the charge in Against Celsus (3.10 to 12). Modern skeptics make the same point with the history of schisms since: the division of East and West, symbolized by the mutual excommunications of 1054; the Reformation and the wars of religion that followed; and the many denominations of the present day. If Jesus prayed for unity so that the world would believe (verse 21), the objection runs, the world's unbelief is his prayer's failure, and Christians' quarrels are the best argument against their claims.

Christians answer from different traditions, and their answers differ as much as their churches do. Origen replied that serious movements, like medicine and philosophy, give rise to schools precisely because they are serious, and that the existence of heresies does not refute the truth. The Catholic Church holds that the unity Christ prayed for subsists in the Catholic Church, while real though imperfect communion exists with other Christians, and it has committed itself to seeking full visible unity (Unitatis Redintegratio, 1964; Ut Unum Sint, 1995). The Orthodox Church holds that unity is given in the one faith and the one Eucharist of the church that has kept the apostolic tradition. Many Protestants distinguish the invisible church, one already in Christ, from its visible divisions, and they hold that unity in the truth of the gospel matters more than institutional union; the Lausanne Covenant (1974) nonetheless affirmed that the church's visible unity in truth is God's purpose and confessed the harm done by needless division. The modern ecumenical movement, from the Edinburgh Missionary Conference of 1910 to the founding of the World Council of Churches in 1948, took this prayer as its charter. Ernst Käsemann (The Testament of Jesus, 1966) argued that the unity in view is unity in the word Jesus gave, not organizational unity, and many evangelical interpreters agree.

All these answers share two points. The prayer is not only a description but a petition, and Christians confess that it is being answered in every age as believers of different nations and cultures recognize one another in Christ. And the church's divisions are a real obstacle to the world's faith, as Jesus' own words imply, so they call for repentance rather than defense. Whether the unity Jesus prayed for must take visible institutional form is a second-order question on which the churches still disagree.

observe: What does Jesus say eternal life is (verse 3), and what has he done to glorify the Father on earth (verse 4)?
What does Jesus ask the Father to do for the disciples in verses 11, 15, and 17, and what does he explicitly not ask (verse 15)?
For whom does Jesus pray in verse 20, and what two purposes does he give for their unity in verses 21 and 23?
interpret: What does it mean that the Father has given people to the Son, and how does that shape the way Jesus prays for them?
How can the disciples be in the world but not of the world, and what makes them different, according to verses 14 to 19?
What kind of unity is modeled on the unity of the Father and the Son, and why would it lead the world to believe?
apply: Jesus defines eternal life as knowing God. How does that change what you expect from your life with God now, not only after death?
Where are you tempted either to withdraw from the world or to blend into it, and what would it look like to be sent into it instead?
Jesus prayed for you by name as one of those who would believe through the apostles' message. How does knowing that affect the way you pray and the way you treat other Christians?
